catalog_quote: In Oirata as in other Indonesian languages accentuation is weak and to a large extent free. ... There are, indeed, a few clearly recognizable principles but, setting aside these, a word may be accentuated in different ways according to its position in a group of words or in a sentence and to the requirements of expressiveness .... The tendency, well-known in the Indonesian language area, to lay the main stress on the penultimate syllable is also met with in Oirata. But this tendency is less strong than the dislike to formative elements being stressed at the cost of stem-syllables. Thus when e.g. a dissyllabic word becomes trisyllabic owing to an added end-vowel, the stress stays on the first syllable: lódon: lódono; wúhur: wúhuru etc. The same is true of other trisyllabic words of which the first syllable is the main stem-syllable: láuse: láusana; túhur: túhurai; námi: námirai; áhur-: áhure; ási: ásile. ... márna is preferred to marana; hátle to hátale; wásne to wásune. But there is also a certain dislike to the presence of more than one fully stressed syllable in one word. This is why compounds consisting of two dissyllabic members are very often reduced to three syllables by means of elimination whereby the stress on the first member is considerably weakened. Thus púnukóno usually becomes pùn'kóno (` indicating secondary stress) ...

new_statements.rule_in_words: Main stress sits on the chief (first) syllable of the stem; in bare disyllabic stems this is the penult, and there is a general penultimate tendency, but suffixes/added final vowels never draw stress off the stem (lódono, wúhuru, láusana, túhurai keep initial stress = antepenult). Vowel syncope (márna < marana, hátle < hátale) frequently reconciles stem stress with penultimate position.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Compounds of two disyllabic members avoid two full stresses: they are usually reduced to three syllables and the first member's stress is weakened to secondary (púnukóno > pùn'kóno, múdukéile > mùd'kéile, nérenána > nèrnána); ´ marks principal and ` secondary stress in his accented text sample; principal-stressed syllables are higher in pitch, no safe statement on pitch of secondary stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Penultimate tendency vs. stem-stress conflict resolved in favour of the stem; syncope forms preferred (márna, hátle, wásne); author stresses that accentuation and pitch properly belong to the sentence/period and gives an accent-marked text passage rather than further word rules.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rules stated explicitly ('accentuation of the separate word'), then extended to distribution of fully/weakly/unstressed syllables over word groups and the sentence; data from fieldwork in Oirata, Kisar, 1933-34.
new_statements.identity_note: de Josselin de Jong (fieldwork 1933-34) describes 'Oirata' of the Oirata villages on southern Kisar = Glottolog oira1263 (ISO oia), the language now written Woirata (Nazarudin) and spoken in Oirata Barat/Oirata Timur; no dialect split is reported. The rule describes 1930s speech; modern Woirata (heavy Meher/Malay contact) is undescribed for stress in anything reachable.

new_statements.relation_note: Not a description of Oirata: Middelkoop 1950 describes Uab Meto (Timorese). But p. 399 quotes de Josselin de Jong 1937 p. 178 on 'het Kisarees' (= Oirata; the footnote points to the Oirata monograph and the page of its Accent section) verbatim. The quotation (a) independently confirms, from a printed source with a text, the wording and the page (p. 178) of one sentence of the 1937 stress passage that the catalog's existing statement was reconstructed from Google Books snippets, and (b) adds the compound-stress detail (one full stress per word; first member weakened). Compatible with the existing 'morphologically determined / penult tendency' statement; no different placement. It also resolv…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The work's own subject is Timorees (Uab Meto/Dawan/Atoni, incl. Amarasi and Amfo'an), NOT Oirata: there, disyllabic stems carry stress on the first syllable, with listed loanword and pa-/pe- exceptions and compound-stress reduction. Its only Oirata content is a verbatim quotation (p. 399, fn. 6) of de Josselin de Jong 1937 p. 178: an Oirata word avoids more than one full stress; compounds of two disyllabic members are reduced to three syllables and the first member's stress is weakened, i.e. the main stress stays on the (stem syllable of the) second member. This is one sentence of the same 1937 accent passage that the existing statement rests on (penultimate tendency overridden by keeping stress on stem syllables rather than formatives); the reading given here is that of the 1937 passage as a whole, which this quotation corroborates.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Per the quoted 1937 sentence, in reduced compounds the first member keeps only a considerably weakened (secondary) stress, the full stress being on the second member (the 1937 original continues with examples pùn'kóno, mùd'kéile, nèrnána, not reproduced by Middelkoop).
new_statements.exceptions: None for Oirata. (For Uab Meto, Middelkoop lists loanwords such as kelak, filuil, hèlanlis, walnemen and pa-/pe- words such as palak, palsai, polis, paleo, palkanis, paililu with second/final-syllable stress, plus kolès, kalin, bukis, sakan, and compound reduction pèn-lèko, nakfatu, totiu.)
new_statements.identity_note: Middelkoop 1950 describes 'Timorees' = Uab Meto / Dawan (Atoni), with Amarasi and Amfo'an dialect forms cited; it refers to Oirata only as 'het Kisarees' via de Josselin de Jong 1937 (Oirata of Kisar). Its initial-stress rule (p. 398) belongs to Uab Meto and must not be attributed to Oirata.
